passage: Outside the tea shop in the kasba, Jeevan picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note. "Finders keepers!" said Rashmi, and two other kids joined in. "Chips! Chips!" Jeevan's fingers closed around the note. He wanted them to like him, and he also knew it was somebody's. "Let's ask the tea shop uncle if anyone lost it," he said, his voice a little shaky. A groan went up and someone rolled their eyes, but Rashmi shrugged. "Fine, ask." Later, when the others had run ahead, Rashmi said quietly, "I didn't feel right about it either."

qa.q: What kind of note did Jeevan pick up?
qa.a: He picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan's voice shaky when he suggested asking the tea shop uncle?
qa.a: He was torn between wanting the group to like him and knowing the note belonged to somebody, and he may have feared their reaction.

qa.q: What small step let Jeevan say no without a fight?
qa.a: He offered a simple alternative, asking the tea shop uncle whether anyone had lost it, instead of lecturing his friends.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have seen that moment?
qa.a: Rashmi joined the cheer at first, but later admitted not feeling right about it either, so was probably quietly relieved that someone said it.

grounding: Illustrates a child torn between friends' finders-keepers pressure and doing right, declining politely.

passage: Last summer, my friends and I found a fifty-rupee note in the dust behind the cricket ground. I'm Dhruv. Straight away Aman shouted, 'Finders keepers! Chips and cold drinks for everyone!' and the others cheered. I wanted to cheer too. Everyone was looking at me, because I was the one holding it. My mouth went dry. I kept thinking of the old watchman, who had been searching the grass all morning. 'I think it might be the watchman's,' I said. 'I'm going to ask him.' Aman groaned and called me a goody-goody. But on the way, Ujjwal fell into step beside me. 'I was thinking the same thing,' he whispered. 'I just didn't want to say it.' The watchman nearly cried when we gave it back.

qa.q: Where did they find the note?
qa.a: In the dust behind the cricket ground.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when everyone looked at the note?
qa.a: Torn and nervous, mouth dry, wanting to fit in but thinking of the watchman.

qa.q: How did Dhruv decline without a fight?
qa.a: By calmly saying it might be the watchman's and going to ask him.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel about Dhruv speaking up?
qa.a: Relieved; he had been thinking the same thing but hadn't dared to say it.

grounding: A child pressured by friends to keep found money politely declines, and one friend is quietly relieved.

passage:
Playground note, by Dilnaz Irani, lunch supervisor.
Near the swings today, a group of Class 5 children found a twenty-rupee note. I heard one shout, 'Finders keepers! Ice lollies!' and three others agreed at once. Vidya, who had picked it up, went very still. She looked from the group to the note and bit her lip. 'We should ask whose it is,' she said quietly. Two of them rolled their eyes. 'Don't be boring.' Vidya didn't argue. She just said, 'I'm giving it to the supervisor,' and walked to me. As she came, I noticed one of the group, Minal, trailing behind and letting out a long breath. The note belonged to a Class 2 child, who got it back before the bell.

qa.q: What did Vidya's stillness and bitten lip show?
qa.a: She felt torn between fitting in with the group and doing what was right.

qa.q: How did Vidya decline without a fight?
qa.a: She said once that they should ask whose it was, didn't argue, and simply walked the note to the supervisor.

qa.q: How might Minal have felt as she trailed behind?
qa.a: Relieved that someone had said it, since Minal let out a long breath.

grounding: A supervisor's note records a girl declining her friends' 'finders keepers' plan and handing in found money.
